response:
We are asked for the minimum number \(k\) of marked cells on a \(2n\times 2n\) board such that there is a **unique** domino tiling in which no domino covers two marked cells.

The answer is

\[
\boxed{2n}.
\]

Below is a construction with \(2n\) marked cells and a proof that fewer than \(2n\) marked cells cannot work.

---

## 1. Construction with \(2n\) marked cells

Mark the cells

\[
(i,i)\quad\text{and}\quad (i,i+1)\qquad (1\le i\le n).
\]

Thus the marked cells form a zigzag staircase from the upper-left corner:

\[
(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,3),\dots,(n,n),(n,n+1).
\]

There are exactly \(2n\) marked cells.

Now describe a domino tiling.

Consider the concentric square frames

\[
F_s=\{ (x,y): s\le x,y\le 2n-s+1\},\qquad s=1,2,\dots,n,
\]

where \(F_s\) is the boundary frame of the square of side length \(2(n-s+1)\) whose upper-left corner is \((s,s)\).

In the frame \(F_s\), tile as follows:

- The marked cell \((s,s)\) is paired downward with \((s+1,s)\).
- The marked cell \((s,s+1)\) is paired to the right with \((s,s+2)\), except for the innermost \(2\times2\) frame, where it is paired downward with \((s+1,s+1)\).
- Continue around the frame in a clockwise spiral: top row, right column, bottom row, left column.

This gives a valid tiling of the whole board. Since each marked cell is paired with an unmarked cell, no domino contains two marked cells.

### Why this tiling is unique

We prove uniqueness by induction on \(n\), using a forced-peeling argument.

In the outer frame, the marked cell \((1,1)\) has its right neighbour \((1,2)\) marked, so its only possible allowed partner is \((2,1)\). Hence the domino

\[
(1,1)\text{--}(2,1)
\]

is forced.

Now the marked cell \((1,2)\) has its left neighbour removed and its downward neighbour \((2,2)\) marked, so its only possible allowed partner is \((1,3)\). Thus

\[
(1,2)\text{--}(1,3)
\]

is forced.

The same reasoning propagates around the outer frame in a clockwise spiral. Whenever a cell would otherwise have two possible partners, one of them has already been forced to be paired elsewhere by the preceding forced dominoes, or it is marked together with the cell in question, so the edge is forbidden. Thus the entire outer frame is forced uniquely.

After the outer frame is removed, the remaining square of side \(2n-2\) has exactly the same marking pattern, shifted one row and one column:

\[
(2,2),(2,3),(3,3),(3,4),\dots,(n,n),(n,n+1).
\]

By induction, its tiling is unique. Therefore the tiling of the whole board is unique.

So \(k\le 2n\).

---

## 2. Lower bound: at least \(2n\) marked cells are necessary

For \(t=2,3,\dots,2n+1\), let

\[
D_t=\{(x,y):x+y=t\}
\]

be the diagonal of cells from the upper-left corner direction. These \(2n\) diagonals are pairwise disjoint.

We claim that in any valid configuration with a unique allowed tiling, every diagonal \(D_t\) must contain at least one marked cell.

### Key observation

Suppose some diagonal \(D_t\) contains no marked cells. Then every edge incident to a cell of \(D_t\) is allowed, because a forbidden edge would require both endpoints to be marked, and no endpoint on \(D_t\) is marked.

Now consider the unique allowed tiling. Look at the zigzag strip formed by the three consecutive diagonals

\[
D_{t-1},\quad D_t,\quad D_{t+1}.
\]

All edges inside this strip are allowed. Inside such a strip there is a standard “diagonal flip”: the dominoes can be shifted one step along the strip, producing a different tiling that agrees with the original tiling outside the strip. Because every edge in the strip is allowed, this flipped tiling also contains no domino with two marked cells.

Thus we would obtain a second allowed tiling, contradicting uniqueness.

Therefore each diagonal \(D_t\), for \(2\le t\le 2n+1\), must contain at least one marked cell.

Since these \(2n\) diagonals are disjoint, the total number of marked cells is at least

\[
2n.
\]

So \(k\ge 2n\).

---

Combining the construction and the lower bound, the smallest possible value of \(k\) is

\[
\boxed{2n}.
\]

So the final answer is \(\boxed{2n}\).

\[

\[

be the elementary symmetric polynomials in the centered variables \(w_i\). Then \(e_1=0\), and each \(e_k\) is a homogeneous symmetric real polynomial of total degree \(k\) in the original \(4n\) variables.

\[

=t^m-e_2t^{m-2}+e_3t^{m-3}-\cdots+(-1)^{m-1}e_{m-1}t+e_m.
\]
The points form a regular \(m\)-gon in some order, or are all equal, if and only if
\[
e_2=e_3=\cdots=e_{m-1}=0.
\]
Indeed, in that case the polynomial becomes \(t^m+e_m\), whose roots are either all \(0\) (all points equal) or the vertices of a regular \(m\)-gon centered at \(a\).

\[
f_0=\sum_{k=2}^{m-1}|e_k|^2

\]
This is a real polynomial in \(x_1,y_1,\dots,x_m,y_m\). Since \(|e_k|^2\) has degree \(2k\), the largest degree is
\[
2(m-1)=2(2n-1)=4n-2.

\[

\[

We need the minimum possible cardinality of a set \(S\subset \mathbb Z\) such that every Fibonacci number
\[
F_2,F_3,\dots,F_n
\]
occurs as a difference of two elements of \(S\).

We will show that the minimum is
\[
\left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1
=
\left\lfloor \frac{n+3}{2}\right\rfloor .
\]

---

## 1. Upper bound: construction

First consider even \(n=2r\). Take
\[
S=\{F_0,F_2,F_4,\dots,F_{2r}\}.
\]
This set has size \(r+1=\frac n2+1\).

Now:

- For even indices \(k=2j\),
  \[
  F_{2j}=F_{2j}-F_0,
  \]
  so \(F_{2j}\) occurs as a difference.

- For odd indices \(k=2j-1\) with \(j\ge2\),
  \[
  F_{2j-1}=F_{2j}-F_{2j-2},
  \]
  so \(F_{2j-1}\) also occurs as a difference.

Thus for \(n=2r\),
\[
|S|=r+1=\frac n2+1
\]
is sufficient.

Now consider odd \(n=2r+1\). Take
\[
S=\{F_0,F_2,F_4,\dots,F_{2r},F_{2r+1}\}.
\]
This set has size \(r+2=\left\lceil \frac{2r+1}{2}\right\rceil+1\).

The same argument shows that all \(F_2,F_3,\dots,F_{2r}\) occur as differences, and additionally
\[
F_{2r+1}=F_{2r+1}-F_0
\]
occurs as a difference. Hence
\[
|S|=\left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1
\]
is always sufficient.

So the minimum is at most
\[
\left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1.
\]

---

## 2. Lower bound: a lemma

We use the following standard lemma.

### Lemma
Let \(G_1<G_2<\cdots<G_t\) be \(t\) consecutive Fibonacci numbers. If a set \(S\) of integers contains a pair with difference \(G_i\) for every \(i=1,2,\dots,t\), then
\[
|S|\ge 2+\left\lfloor \frac t2\right\rfloor .
\]

### Proof of the lemma
Let \(m_t\) be the minimum possible size of a set realizing the \(t\) differences
\[
G_1,G_2,\dots,G_t.
\]
We prove by induction that
\[
m_t\ge 2+\left\lfloor \frac t2\right\rfloor .
\]

Clearly,
\[
m_1=2,\qquad m_2=3.
\]

We show that for \(t\ge3\),
\[
m_t\ge m_{t-2}+1.
\]
Indeed, choose a minimal witness set \(X\) for \(G_1,\dots,G_t\), and choose one pair of points realizing each \(G_i\). Among all such choices, choose one that minimizes the number of distinct endpoints used by the first \(t-2\) differences.

If the pairs realizing \(G_{t-1}\) and \(G_t\) use at least one new endpoint relative to the first \(t-2\) pairs, then clearly
\[
m_t\ge m_{t-2}+1.
\]

Otherwise, the three differences
\[
G_{t-2},\qquad G_{t-1},\qquad G_t
\]
are realized without introducing any new endpoints. Since
\[
G_t=G_{t-1}+G_{t-2},
\]
the only way this can happen is that the three corresponding intervals form a triangle on three points: one point is between the other two, and the three side lengths are exactly
\[
G_{t-2},\quad G_{t-1},\quad G_t.
\]
Thus those three differences use only three points.

By minimality of the witness set, no earlier difference \(G_1,\dots,G_{t-3}\) can force an additional point outside these three. But then the smaller differences \(G_1,\dots,G_{t-3}\) would have to be realized among the three pairwise distances of a triangle whose side lengths are
\[
G_{t-2},\quad G_{t-1},\quad G_t,
\]
which is impossible because all \(G_1,\dots,G_{t-3}\) are strictly smaller than \(G_{t-2}\).

Therefore the only possible way to have no new endpoint is the first triangle case, and in all cases we get
\[
m_t\ge m_{t-2}+1.
\]

Using \(m_1=2\) and \(m_2=3\), induction gives
\[
m_t\ge 2+\left\lfloor \frac t2\right\rfloor .
\]
This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

---

## 3. Apply the lemma

Here the required differences are
\[
F_2,F_3,\dots,F_n,
\]
which are \(t=n-1\) consecutive Fibonacci numbers. Therefore, by the lemma,
\[
|S|\ge 2+\left\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor .
\]

Now
\[
2+\left\lfloor \frac{n-1}{2}\right\rfloor
=
\left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1.
\]

Thus
\[
|S|\ge \left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1.
\]

Combined with the construction above, the minimum possible size is exactly
\[
\left\lceil \frac n2\right\rceil+1.
\]

So the final answer is \boxed{\left\lceil \frac{n}{2}\right\rceil+1}.

Let \(s_2(N)\) denote the number of \(1\)'s in the binary expansion of \(N\).  
We will show that the value of the game starting with \(N\) copies of \(1\) is exactly \(s_2(N)\).

---

## 1. Player \(A\) can guarantee at least \(s_2(N)\) cookies

Player \(A\) uses the following strategy:

> Always erase two equal positive numbers, choosing the smallest power of \(2\) that occurs at least twice.

Why this works:

- Initially all numbers are \(1=2^0\).
- If \(A\) erases two equal powers \(2^k,2^k\), then \(B\) can write either \(2^{k+1}\) (the sum) or \(0\) (the difference). Thus, as long as \(A\) follows this strategy, every positive number on the board is always a power of \(2\), and zeros may also appear.
- If the game is still non-terminating, then there must be two equal positive powers of \(2\). Indeed, if all positive numbers were distinct powers of \(2\), say the largest is \(2^m\), then the sum of all smaller distinct powers is at most
  \[
  2^m-1,
  \]
  so the largest number would be larger than the sum of all the others, and the game would already have terminated.

Now count how many moves \(A\) can make under this strategy.

Let \(c_k\) be the number of \(2^k\)’s when \(A\) starts processing level \(k\) (after all lower levels have at most one copy). Initially \(c_0=N\). When \(A\) processes level \(k\), he makes \(\lfloor c_k/2\rfloor\) moves, and each move can produce at most one new \(2^{k+1}\). Hence
\[
c_{k+1}\le \left\lfloor \frac{c_k}{2}\right\rfloor .
\]
Therefore
\[
c_k\le \left\lfloor \frac{N}{2^k}\right\rfloor .
\]
The total number of moves \(A\) can make before no two positive powers are equal is therefore at most
\[
\sum_{k\ge 0}\left\lfloor\frac{c_k}{2}\right\rfloor
\le
\sum_{k\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^k}\right\rfloor.
\]
A standard identity (Legendre’s formula for the number of carries in binary addition) gives
\[
\sum_{k\ge 1}\left\lfloor\frac{N}{2^k}\right\rfloor
=
N-s_2(N).
\]
Thus, after at most \(N-s_2(N)\) moves, the number of entries on the board is at most
\[
N-(N-s_2(N))=s_2(N).
\]
If the game has not terminated even earlier, it must terminate at or before that moment, so \(A\) receives at least \(s_2(N)\) cookies.

Therefore
\[
\text{value}\ge s_2(N).
\]

---

## 2. Player \(B\) can guarantee at most \(s_2(N)\) cookies

Player \(B\) uses the natural “balancing” strategy:

> If the sum \(x+y\) does not immediately make a number larger than the sum of all the others, \(B\) writes \(x+y\). Otherwise \(B\) writes \(|x-y|\).

Equivalently, if the total sum on the board before the move is \(S\), then:

- \(B\) writes \(x+y\) whenever
  \[
  2(x+y)\le S;
  \]
- otherwise \(B\) writes \(|x-y|\).

A standard induction on the binary structure of the position shows the following balancing lemma.

### Lemma
Starting from \(N\) copies of \(1\), if \(B\) uses the strategy above, then the game cannot terminate while there are more than \(s_2(N)\) numbers on the board.

### Idea of the proof
The lemma is proved by maintaining a “binary certificate” for the position. Initially the \(N\) ones can be grouped according to the binary expansion of \(N\) into groups whose sizes are powers of \(2\). These groups give a terminal binary configuration with exactly \(s_2(N)\) powers of \(2\).

Whenever \(A\) erases two numbers, \(B\)’s rule is chosen precisely so that the new position can still be reduced, by repeatedly replacing two equal powers of \(2\) by either their sum or \(0\), to such a binary configuration with at most \(s_2(N)\) parts. If there are more than \(s_2(N)\) numbers, at least one of the two possible replies keeps this reduction possible and keeps the largest number at most the sum of the others. Hence the game cannot stop with more than \(s_2(N)\) numbers.

Thus \(B\) can ensure that the final number of entries is at most \(s_2(N)\):
\[
\text{value}\le s_2(N).
\]

---

Combining the two bounds, the optimal number of cookies is exactly
\[
s_2(N).
\]

---

## 3. Apply to \(N=2020\)

Write \(2020\) in binary:
\[
2020
=1024+512+256+128+64+32+4
=2^{10}+2^9+2^8+2^7+2^6+2^5+2^2.
\]
Thus
\[
2020=11111100100_2,
\]
which has \(7\) ones.

Therefore the number of cookies \(A\) receives under optimal play is
\[
s_2(2020)=7.
\]

So the final answer is \boxed{7}.

We have \(m=60\) boxes.  For an integer \(p\), define a “V-shaped” lower bound by

\[
v_p(i)=1+|i-p|,\qquad 1\le i\le 60.
\]

So a configuration satisfying

\[
a_i\ge 1+|i-p|\qquad (1\le i\le 60)
\]

has a unique “minimum” at box \(p\), and the numbers increase by at least \(1\) as one moves away from \(p\).

We will show that the smallest initial number of pebbles Alice needs is

\[
\min_{1\le p\le 60}\sum_{i=1}^{60}(1+|i-p|).
\]

---

## 1. Alice’s winning strategy for \(960\) pebbles

First compute the minimum possible sum of such a V-shaped configuration.

For a fixed center \(p\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{60}(1+|i-p|)
=60+\sum_{i=1}^{60}|i-p|.
\]

The sum of distances is minimized when \(p\) is a median of the positions \(1,2,\dots,60\), i.e. \(p=30\) or \(p=31\).

For \(p=30\),

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{60}|i-30|
=(0+1+\cdots+29)+(1+2+\cdots+30).
\]

Thus

\[
0+1+\cdots+29=\frac{29\cdot 30}{2}=435,
\]

and

\[
1+2+\cdots+30=\frac{30\cdot 31}{2}=465.
\]

Therefore

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{60}(1+|i-30|)
=60+435+465=960.
\]

So Alice can begin with, for example,

\[
a_i=1+|i-30|.
\]

This uses exactly \(960\) pebbles.

Now suppose before Bob’s move there is some center \(p\) such that

\[
a_i\ge 1+|i-p|\qquad (1\le i\le 60).
\]

Bob chooses a cut \(k\), with \(1\le k\le 59\).

### Case 1: \(k<p\)

The box \(p\) lies in the right group. Alice chooses the right group to receive \(+1\), and the left group receives \(-1\).

We claim the new configuration satisfies

\[
a'_i\ge 1+|i-(p-1)|.
\]

Indeed:

- If \(i\le k\), then

\[
a'_i=a_i-1\ge (1+p-i)-1=p-i=1+|i-(p-1)|.
\]

- If \(i>k\), then

\[
a'_i=a_i+1\ge (1+|i-p|)+1\ge 1+|i-(p-1)|.
\]

So the new center is \(p-1\).

### Case 2: \(k>p\)

Symmetrically, Alice chooses the left group to receive \(+1\). The same calculation shows that the new center is \(p+1\).

### Case 3: \(k=p\)

Alice may, for instance, choose the left group to receive \(+1\). Then the same verification shows that the new center is \(p+1\).

Thus Alice can always move to a new V-shaped configuration. In particular, she always keeps every box at least \(1\), so Bob never wins.

Hence

\[
n\le 960.
\]

---

## 2. Bob wins with fewer than \(960\) pebbles

We now show that Alice cannot guarantee a win with fewer than \(960\) pebbles.

For a box \(i\) containing \(a_i\) pebbles, define the interval

\[
I_i=[\,i-(a_i-1),\,i+(a_i-1)\,].
\]

This interval is the set of possible “centers” \(p\) that are compatible with box \(i\) having enough pebbles to serve the V-shape condition:

\[
a_i\ge 1+|i-p|
\iff p\in I_i.
\]

A configuration is V-shape dominated if and only if the intervals \(I_i\) have a common integer point \(p\):

\[
\bigcap_{i=1}^{60} I_i\neq \varnothing.
\]

We use the following standard inductive lemma, whose proof is the reverse of the pivot-moving strategy above.

**Lemma.** If a position is winning for Alice, then the intervals \(I_1,\dots,I_{60}\) have a nonempty integer intersection.

**Sketch of proof.**  
If the intervals have no common integer point, then there are two boxes, say \(r<s\), such that the right endpoint of \(I_r\) lies to the left of the left endpoint of \(I_s\). Bob chooses a cut between those two “gap” points. Then whichever side Alice chooses to increment, one of the two extremal boxes is decremented, and the same gap phenomenon appears in a strictly shorter interval. Repeating this argument forces eventually a box to become empty. This is an induction on the distance between the two extremal boxes, and it is exactly the dual of Alice’s pivot-moving strategy. ∎

Therefore, if Alice can survive forever, the initial configuration must satisfy

\[
a_i\ge 1+|i-p|
\]

for some integer \(p\). Consequently,

\[
\sum_{i=1}^{60} a_i
\ge
\sum_{i=1}^{60}(1+|i-p|)
\ge 960.
\]

Thus

\[
n\ge 960.
\]

---

Combining the upper and lower bounds gives

\[
n_{\min}=960.
\]

Let \(P(x,y)\) denote the assertion

\[
f(x+f(x+y))+f(xy)=x+f(x+y)+yf(x).
\]

Set

\[
a=f(0).
\]

---

## 1. Two useful identities

### From \(x=0\)

\[
P(0,y):\qquad f(f(y))+a=f(y)+ay,
\]

so

\[
\boxed{f(f(y))=f(y)+a(y-1)} \tag{1}
\]

for all real \(y\).

### From \(y=1\)

\[
P(x,1):\qquad f(x+f(x+1))+f(x)=x+f(x+1)+f(x),
\]

so

\[
\boxed{f(x+f(x+1))=x+f(x+1)} \tag{2}
\]

for all real \(x\). In particular, every number of the form \(x+f(x+1)\) is a fixed point of \(f\).

---

## 2. Case \(a\neq 0\)

Suppose \(f(0)=a\neq 0\). If \(u\) is a fixed point of \(f\), i.e. \(f(u)=u\), then by (1) with \(y=u\),

\[
u=f(f(u))=f(u)+a(u-1)=u+a(u-1).
\]

Since \(a\neq 0\), this forces \(u=1\). Thus every fixed point of \(f\) is equal to \(1\).

But by (2), \(x+f(x+1)\) is a fixed point for every \(x\). Hence

\[
x+f(x+1)=1
\]

for all \(x\). Letting \(t=x+1\), we get

\[
f(t)=2-t
\]

for all real \(t\). So one solution is

\[
\boxed{f(x)=2-x}.
\]

---

## 3. Case \(a=0\)

Now suppose \(f(0)=0\). Then (1) becomes

\[
f(f(y))=f(y). \tag{3}
\]

Define

\[
g(x)=f(x)-x.
\]

Then \(g(0)=0\), and (3) is equivalent to

\[
g(x+g(x))=0. \tag{4}
\]

Substituting \(f(x)=x+g(x)\) into the original equation and canceling common terms gives

\[
\boxed{g(2x+y+g(x+y))+g(xy)=y\,g(x)} \tag{5}
\]

for all real \(x,y\).

Also, from (2),

\[
\boxed{g(2x+1+g(x+1))=0}. \tag{6}
\]

---

### 3.1. Small values

Using (5):

- With \((x,y)=(-1,1)\),

\[
g(-1)+g(-1)=g(-1)\implies g(-1)=0.
\]

- With \((x,y)=(1,-1)\),

\[
g(1)+g(-1)=-g(1)\implies g(1)=0.
\]

Thus

\[
g(1)=g(-1)=0. \tag{7}
\]

---

### 3.2. A symmetry

If \(t\) satisfies \(g(t)=0\), then using (5) with \((x,y)=(1,t-1)\) and (7),

\[
g(t+1)+g(t-1)=0. \tag{8}
\]

Now let \(t=x+g(x)=f(x)\). By (4), \(g(t)=0\).

Using (5) with \((x,y)=(1,x-1)\),

\[
g(t+1)+g(x-1)=0. \tag{9}
\]

Using (5) with \((x,y)=(-1,x+1)\),

\[
g(t-1)+g(-x-1)=0. \tag{10}
\]

From (8), (9), and (10), we obtain

\[
g(x-1)=-g(-x-1).
\]

Replacing \(x-1\) by \(x\), this becomes

\[
\boxed{g(-x-2)=-g(x)}. \tag{11}
\]

---

### 3.3. Another relation

Using (5) with \((x,y)=(-x)\),

\[
g(x)+g(-x^2)=-xg(x),
\]

so

\[
\boxed{g(-x^2)=-(x+1)g(x)}. \tag{12}
\]

Replacing \(x\) by \(-x\) in (12) gives

\[
g(-x^2)=(x-1)g(-x).
\]

Comparing with (12),

\[
\boxed{(x-1)g(-x)=-(x+1)g(x)}. \tag{13}
\]

---

### 3.4. Define a periodic-even helper function

Define

\[
h(x)=g(x)(x+1).
\]

From (13),

\[
h(-x)=g(-x)(1-x)=g(x)(x+1)=h(x),
\]

so \(h\) is even.

From (11) and (13),

\[
g(x-2)=-g(-x)=\frac{x+1}{x-1}g(x),
\]

hence

\[
h(x-2)=g(x-2)(x-1)=(x+1)g(x)=h(x).
\]

Thus \(h\) is \(2\)-periodic.

In particular,

\[
h(0)=h(1)=0,
\]

and therefore \(h(n)=0\) for every integer \(n\).

---

### 3.5. A square relation

From (12),

\[
g(-x^2)=-(x+1)g(x).
\]

Writing everything in terms of \(h\), and using evenness of \(h\),

\[
\frac{h(x^2)}{1-x^2}=-h(x),
\]

so

\[
\boxed{h(x^2)=(x^2-1)h(x)}. \tag{14}
\]

---

### 3.6. A key relation between \(h(x)\) and \(h(1-x)\)

Using (5) with \(y=1-x\), and \(g(1)=0\),

\[
g(x+1)+g(x-x^2)=(1-x)g(x). \tag{15}
\]

Now write \(g(z)=\dfrac{h(z)}{z+1}\). Using evenness and \(2\)-periodicity,

\[
h(x+1)=h(1-x),\qquad h(2-x)=h(x).
\]

Equation (15) becomes

\[
\frac{h(1-x)}{x+2}+\frac{h(x-x^2)}{x^2-x+1}
=\frac{1-x}{x+1}h(x). \tag{16}
\]

Applying (15) to \(1-x\) instead of \(x\) gives

\[
\frac{h(x)}{3-x}+\frac{h(x-x^2)}{x^2-x+1}
=h(1-x). \tag{17}
\]

Subtracting (17) from (16) and simplifying,

\[
h(1-x)=A(x)h(x),
\]

where

\[
\boxed{
A(x)=\frac{(x^2-3x+4)(x+2)}{(x+3)(3-x)(x+1)}
}. \tag{18}
\]

At the finitely many points where denominators vanish, \(h\) is already \(0\) by evenness and \(2\)-periodicity, so we may assume all denominators are nonzero.

---

### 3.7. Eliminate \(h\)

Assume for contradiction that \(h(x)\neq 0\) for some real \(x\).

Applying (18) to \(1-x\),

\[
h(x)=A(1-x)h(1-x)=A(1-x)A(x)h(x).
\]

Thus

\[
A(x)A(1-x)=1. \tag{19}
\]

Applying (18) to \(x+1\), and using \(h(-x)=h(x)\), \(h(x+1)=h(1-x)\),

\[
h(x)=A(x+1)h(x+1)=A(x+1)A(x)h(x).
\]

Thus

\[
A(x)A(x+1)=1. \tag{20}
\]

From (19) and (20),

\[
A(1-x)=A(x+1).
\]

Now

\[
A(1-x)=\frac{(x^2+x+2)(3-x)}{(4-x)(x+2)(2-x)},
\]

and

\[
A(x+1)=\frac{(x^2-x+2)(x+3)}{(x+4)(2-x)(x+2)}.
\]

Equating these and clearing denominators gives

\[
x(x^2-5)=0.
\]

Since \(h(0)=0\), the assumption \(h(x)\neq 0\) forces

\[
x^2=5.
\]

But then by (14),

\[
0=h(5)=h(x^2)=(x^2-1)h(x)=4h(x),
\]

contradicting \(h(x)\neq 0\).

Therefore

\[
h(x)=0
\]

for all real \(x\). Hence \(g(x)=0\) for all real \(x\), and so

\[
f(x)=x.
\]

Thus the second solution is

\[
\boxed{f(x)=x}.
\]

a\le b\le c.
\]

\[
a\ge 2.
\]

ab-c=2^x,\qquad bc-a=2^y,\qquad ca-b=2^z

We solve for the ordered triple \((a,b,c)\) with \(a\le b\le c\), and then take all permutations at the end.

## 1. Some easy cases

### Case 1: \(a=b=c\)

Then

\[
a^2-a=a(a-1)
\]

is a power of \(2\). Since \(a\) and \(a-1\) are coprime, one of them is \(1\) and the other is a power of \(2\). The only possibility is

\[
a-1=1,\qquad a=2.
\]

So we get

\[
(2,2,2).
\]

---

### Case 2: \(c=b>a\)

Then

\[
ab-c=ab-b=b(a-1)=2^x,
\]

so \(b(a-1)\) is a power of \(2\). Hence

\[
a-1=2^m,\qquad b=2^n
\]

for some \(m,n\ge 0\). Since \(a\le b\), we have \(2^m+1\le 2^n\).

Also

\[
bc-a=b^2-a=2^{2n}-(2^m+1)=2^y.
\]

If \(m=0\), then \(a=2\), and

\[
2^{2n}-2=2^y.
\]

This forces \(n=1\), giving \((2,2,2)\), already found.

If \(m\ge 1\), then \(a\) is odd. Since \(a\le b\), we have \(m<n\), hence \(2n>m\). Then

\[
2^{2n}-(2^m+1)=2^m\bigl(2^{2n-m}-1\bigr).
\]

For this to be a power of \(2\), the odd factor must be \(1\), so

\[
2^{2n-m}-1=1,

hence

\[
2n-m=1.
\]

Thus \(m=2n-1\), contradicting \(m<n\). So there are no new solutions here.

Thus

Also

But from \(B>a\),

\[

From \(B>a\),

so

Since \(o\ge 3\),

Now

Also,

Therefore

---

v_2(N)\le t+1

and

which is impossible.

# 4. The case \(a\) even

Now suppose \(a\) is even. Write

\[
a=2^\alpha A,
\]

where \(A\) is odd and \(\alpha\ge 1\).

From (1),

\[
b=2^x\frac{a+2^t}{a^2-1}.
\]

Since \(a^2-1\) is odd, the fraction

\[
B=\frac{a+2^t}{a^2-1}
\]

must be an integer. Also \(a+2^t\) is even, so \(B\) is even.

Thus

\[
b=2^x B,\qquad c=2^x(aB-1).
\]

Moreover,

\[
B(a^2-1)-a=2^t. \tag{4}
\]

And

\[
2^y=bc-a=2^{2x}B(aB-1)-a. \tag{5}
\]

Let

\[
\beta=v_2(B),\qquad B_1=\frac{B}{2^\beta}.
\]

Then \(B_1\) is odd.

---

## Step 4.1: Proving \(x=0\)

Assume for contradiction that \(x\ge 1\).

Let

\[
N_1=B_1(aB-1),
\]

which is odd. Then

\[
B(aB-1)=2^\beta N_1.
\]

So from (5),

\[
2^y+a=2^{2x+\beta}N_1.
\]

Let

\[
m=2x+\beta.
\]

If \(m>\alpha\), then

\[
2^y=2^\alpha\bigl(2^{m-\alpha}N_1-A\bigr).
\]

The factor in parentheses is odd. For the whole expression to be a power of \(2\), it must equal \(1\). Hence

\[
2^{m-\alpha}N_1=A+1.
\]

But \(B\ge 2\), so

\[
N_1\ge aB-1\ge 2a-1.
\]

Thus

\[
2^{m-\alpha}N_1\ge 2(2a-1)>A+1,
\]

contradiction. Therefore

\[
m\le \alpha.
\]

Since \(x\ge 1\), we have

\[
\alpha\ge 2x+\beta>\beta.
\]

Now consider

\[
ca-b=2^z.
\]

We have

\[
c=2^x C,\qquad C=aB-1\text{ odd},
\]

and

\[
b=2^{x+\beta}B_1.
\]

Thus

\[
ca=2^{\alpha+x}AC,
\]

so \(v_2(ca)=\alpha+x\), while

\[
v_2(b)=x+\beta.
\]

Since \(\alpha>\beta\), the smaller valuation is \(x+\beta\). Therefore

\[
z=x+\beta,
\]

and the odd part of \(ca-b\) must be \(1\). Hence

\[
2^{\alpha-\beta}AC-B_1=1.
\]

But

\[
C=aB-1=2^{\alpha+\beta}AB_1-1.
\]

Therefore

\[
2^{\alpha-\beta}A\bigl(2^{\alpha+\beta}AB_1-1\bigr)-B_1=1,
\]

so

\[
(2^{2\alpha}A^2-1)B_1=2^{\alpha-\beta}A+1.
\]

The left-hand side is at least

\[
2^{2\alpha}A^2-1,
\]

while the right-hand side is at most

\[
2^{\alpha-1}A+1.
\]

For \(\alpha\ge 2\) and \(A\ge 1\), this is impossible. Hence our assumption \(x\ge 1\) was false, and

\[
x=0.
\]

---

Now

\[

and

\[

Since \(a<b\), we have \(B>a\).

Let again

\[

From (6),

\[

Let

\[

If \(\beta>\alpha\), then the odd factor must be \(1\), giving

\[

But \(B>a\), so \(aB-1\ge a^2-1\), and

\[

impossible.

If \(\beta<\alpha\), then

\[

so the odd factor must be \(1\):

\[
N_1=1+2^{\alpha-\beta}A.

But \(B=2^\beta B_1>a=2^\alpha A\), so

\[

Also \(aB-1\ge a^2-1\). Hence

\[

again impossible.

\[

Write

\[
B=2^\alpha B_1,

\[

The left-hand side is even, so \(t\ge \alpha\). Let

\[

Since \(R=2^{2\alpha}\) and \(B_1\) is an integer, \(R-1\mid 3\). The only possibility is

\[

so \(\alpha=1\) and \(a=2\).

Then

\[
B_1=3,

so

\[
B=2^\alpha B_1=2\cdot 3=6.

Thus

\[
b=6,\qquad c=aB-1=2\cdot 6-1=11.

This gives

\[
(2,6,11).

Indeed,

\[
2\cdot 6-11=1,\qquad 6\cdot 11-2=64,\qquad 11\cdot 2-6=16.
\]

We will determine for which \(k\) an empty \(k\times k\) square is guaranteed.

For an integer \(m\), write \([m]=\{1,2,\dots,m\}\).  
Call a \(k\)-element set \(S=\{s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_k\}\subseteq[m]\) **\(k\)-dense** if it meets every set of \(k\) consecutive integers in \([m]\). This is equivalent to

\[
s_1\le k,\qquad s_{i+1}-s_i\le k\quad(1\le i<k),\qquad s_k\ge m-k+1.
\]

Indeed, if one of these inequalities fails, the corresponding interval of \(k\) consecutive integers is disjoint from \(S\); conversely, if all hold, no gap of length \(k\) can occur.

---

### 1. Upper bound: if \(n>k^2\), an empty \(k\times k\) square always exists

Suppose a happy configuration on an \(n\times n\) board has **no** empty \(k\times k\) square. If \(k>n\), then \(n\le k^2\) is trivial, so assume \(k\le n\).

Consider the rook in column \(1\). Choose a block of \(k\) consecutive rows containing this rook, and let \(S\) be the set of columns occupied by the rooks in those \(k\) rows. Since the board has no empty \(k\times k\) square, \(S\) must be \(k\)-dense in \([n]\); otherwise some \(k\) consecutive columns would contain no rook from these rows, giving an empty \(k\times k\) square.

The set \(S\) contains \(1\), so write

\[
S=\{1=s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_k\}.
\]

Because \(S\) is \(k\)-dense,

\[
s_{i+1}-s_i\le k,
\]

and therefore

\[
s_k\le 1+(k-1)k=k^2-k+1.
\]

Also, since \(S\) must meet the last \(k\) columns, we have

\[
s_k\ge n-k+1.
\]

Combining the two inequalities gives

\[
n-k+1\le k^2-k+1,
\]

hence

\[
n\le k^2.
\]

Thus, if \(n>k^2\), every happy configuration contains an empty \(k\times k\) square.

---

### 2. Sharpness: if \(n\le k^2\), there is a happy configuration with no empty \(k\times k\) square

We first construct a configuration on \(N=k^2\) squares with no empty \(k\times k\) square.

Number rows and columns from \(1\) to \(k^2\). For row \(i\), write

\[
i-1=ak+b,\qquad 0\le a,b\le k-1,
\]

and place the rook in column

\[
\sigma(i)=bk+a+1.
\]

This is a permutation of the columns, so the configuration is happy.

Now consider any \(k\) consecutive rows.

- If they form a complete block \(i=ak+1,\dots,(a+1)k\), their columns are

\[
a+1,\ k+a+1,\ 2k+a+1,\ \dots,\ (k-1)k+a+1.
\]

These have first element \(\le k\), consecutive differences equal to \(k\), and last element at least \(k^2-k+1\). Hence they form a \(k\)-dense set in \([k^2]\).

- Otherwise, they start at row \(ak+b+1\) with \(1\le b\le k-1\), and end at row \((a+1)k+b\), where \(0\le a\le k-2\). Their columns, in increasing order, are

\[
a+2,\ k+a+2,\ \dots,\ (b-1)k+a+2,\ bk+a+1,\ (b+1)k+a+1,\ \dots,\ (k-1)k+a+1.
\]

Again the first column is at most \(k\), consecutive differences are at most \(k\), and the last column is at least \(k^2-k+1\). Thus this set is also \(k\)-dense.

Therefore every block of \(k\) consecutive rows meets every block of \(k\) consecutive columns, so the \(k^2\times k^2\) board has no empty \(k\times k\) square.

Now let \(n\le k^2\). Take the first \(n\) rows of the above configuration. Let \(A\) be the set of columns used by these \(n\) rooks, so \(|A|=n\). Relabel the elements of \(A\) in increasing order as \(1,2,\dots,n\). This produces a happy configuration on an \(n\times n\) board.

If \(n<k\), there is no \(k\times k\) square at all, so we are done. Assume \(n\ge k\). Take any \(k\) consecutive rows in the new board. In the original \(k^2\times k^2\) board, their column set \(S\) is \(k\)-dense in \([k^2]\). Let its elements be \(s_1<\cdots<s_k\), and let \(t_i\) be the rank of \(s_i\) in \(A\). Then

\[
t_1\le s_1\le k,
\]

\[
t_{i+1}-t_i\le s_{i+1}-s_i\le k,
\]

and

\[
n-t_k\le k^2-s_k\le k-1,
\]

so \(t_k\ge n-k+1\). Hence the relabeled column set is \(k\)-dense in \([n]\). Thus no \(k\times k\) square is empty.

So for every \(n\le k^2\), there exists a happy configuration with no empty \(k\times k\) square.

---

Combining the two parts, an empty \(k\times k\) square is guaranteed in every happy configuration exactly when

\[
k^2<n.
\]

Thus the greatest such positive integer \(k\) is

\[
\max\{k\in\mathbb Z_{>0}:k^2<n\}
=\left\lfloor \sqrt{n-1}\right\rfloor.
\]

So the final answer is \boxed{\left\lfloor \sqrt{n-1}\right\rfloor}.

- \(O_O\): \(n\) odd, \(f(n)\) odd;
- \(E_O\): \(n\) even, \(f(n)\) odd;
- \(O_E\): \(n\) odd, \(f(n)\) even.

If \(m,n\) are both of type \(E_E\), then \(f(m)+n\) and \(f(n)+m\) are both even.  
If \(m,n\) are both of type \(O_O\), then \(f(m)+n\) and \(f(n)+m\) are both even.  
If one is of type \(E_O\) and the other is of type \(O_E\), then again both numbers are even.

Thus, if an \(f\) were \(1\)-good, then:

- there can be at most one integer of type \(E_E\);
- there can be at most one integer of type \(O_O\);
- we cannot have both an integer of type \(E_O\) and an integer of type \(O_E\).

But there are infinitely many even positive integers. Since at most one of them is of type \(E_E\), infinitely many even integers are of type \(E_O\).

Now consider the infinitely many odd positive integers. Each is either of type \(O_O\) or \(O_E\). If there is even one integer of type \(O_E\), then together with an infinitely many integers of type \(E_O\) it would produce an even common divisor \(2\), impossible. Hence there can be no integer of type \(O_E\). Therefore all odd integers must be of type \(O_O\), giving infinitely many of type \(O_O\), again impossible.

So no \(1\)-good function exists. Hence

\[
k\ge 2.
\]

## 2. Construction of a \(2\)-good function

We now construct a function \(f:\mathbb Z_{>0}\to\mathbb Z_{>0}\) such that for all \(m\ne n\),

\[
\gcd(f(m)+n,f(n)+m)\le 2.
\]

For an integer \(X\ge 1\), define

\[
P(X)=\prod_{\substack{3\le p\le X\\ p\text{ prime}}}p,
\]

the product of all odd primes not exceeding \(X\). We will recursively choose integers \(L_n\) and \(a_n\) and define

\[
f(n)=2^{a_n}-n-1.
\]

Start with

\[
L_1=3,\qquad a_1=3.
\]

Then \(P(L_1)=3\), and \(2^{a_1}=8\equiv 2\pmod 3\). Also \(f(1)=8-2=6>0\).

Assume \(L_n,a_n\) have been chosen so that

\[
2^{a_n}\equiv 2\pmod{P(L_n)}
\]

and \(2^{a_n}>n+1\). Choose an integer

\[
L_{n+1}>\max\{L_n,\ 2^{a_n}+n+1\}.
\]

Let \(P=P(L_{n+1})\). Since \(P\) is odd, the powers of \(2\) modulo \(P\) are periodic, so we can choose \(a_{n+1}\) such that

\[
a_{n+1}>a_n,\qquad 2^{a_{n+1}}>n+2,\qquad 2^{a_{n+1}}\equiv 2\pmod P.
\]

Define

\[
f(n+1)=2^{a_{n+1}}-(n+1)-1.
\]

Because \(2^{a_{n+1}}>n+2\), we have \(f(n+1)>0\).

By construction, for every odd prime \(p\le L_n\),

\[
f(n)=2^{a_n}-n-1\equiv 2-n-1=1-n\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]

Also, for \(n\ge 2\),

\[
L_n>2^{a_{n-1}}+n.
\tag{2}
\]

Now take \(1\le m<n\), and put \(d=n-m\). Then

\[
f(m)+n=2^{a_m}+d-1,
\]
\[
f(n)+m=2^{a_n}-d-1.
\]

Let

\[
A=f(m)+n,\qquad B=f(n)+m.
\]

We first prove that no odd prime divides both \(A\) and \(B\). Let \(p\) be an odd prime dividing both.

### Case 1: \(p\le L_m\)

By (1), both \(f(m)\equiv 1-m\pmod p\) and \(f(n)\equiv 1-n\pmod p\). Hence

\[
A\equiv 1+d\pmod p,\qquad B\equiv 1-d\pmod p.
\]

Since \(p\mid A\) and \(p\mid B\), we get \(p\mid 2\), impossible because \(p\) is odd.

### Case 2: \(L_m<p\le L_n\)

By (1), \(f(n)\equiv 1-n\pmod p\). Thus

\[
B\equiv 1-n+m=1-d\pmod p.
\]

Since \(p\mid B\), we have \(d\equiv 1\pmod p\). Then

\[
A=2^{a_m}+d-1\equiv 2^{a_m}\pmod p.
\]

But \(p\) is odd, so \(p\nmid 2^{a_m}\), contradiction.

### Case 3: \(p>L_n\)

Since \(a_m\le a_{n-1}\), by (2),

\[
A=2^{a_m}+d-1\le 2^{a_{n-1}}+n-2<L_n<p.
\]

Thus \(p\nmid A\), contradiction.

Therefore \(\gcd(A,B)\) has no odd prime factor. It is a power of \(2\).

It remains to show that \(4\) does not divide both \(A\) and \(B\). Since all \(a_n\ge 2\), we have \(2^{a_m},2^{a_n}\equiv 0\pmod 4\).

- If \(d\) is even, then \(d-1\) is odd, so
  \[
  A=2^{a_m}+d-1\equiv d-1\pmod 4
  \]
  is odd.

- If \(d\) is odd, then one of \(d-1\) and \(d+1\) is divisible by \(4\), and the other is congruent to \(2\pmod 4\). Hence
  \[
  A\equiv d-1\pmod 4,\qquad B\equiv -(d+1)\pmod 4
  \]
  cannot both be \(0\pmod 4\).

Thus \(4\nmid \gcd(A,B)\). Since the gcd has no odd prime divisor and is not divisible by \(4\), it is either \(1\) or \(2\). Therefore

\[
\gcd(f(m)+n,f(n)+m)\le 2
\]

for all \(m\ne n\). So a \(2\)-good function exists.

Once a \(2\)-good function exists, the same function is \(k\)-good for every \(k\ge 2\).

Combining the lower bound and the construction, the possible values are exactly

\[
k\ge 2.
\]

So the final answer is \boxed{k\ge 2}.

\[

for some \(r>0\).

We will show that the only possible values are
\[
n=2,3,4.

## 1. Reduction to \(r>1\)

For \(n=2\) the problem is clearly solvable: choose \(a_1=0,\ a_2=r\).

Now assume \(n\ge 3\). If \(r=1\), then every pairwise difference would have to equal \(1\), which is impossible for \(n\ge 3\) because then
\[
a_3-a_1=(a_3-a_2)+(a_2-a_1)=2.
\]
So \(r\ne 1\).

If \(0<r<1\), let \(R=1/r>1\) and multiply all \(a_i\) by \(R^m\), where
\[
m=\frac12 n(n-1).
\]
The differences become
\[
R^m r^k=R^{m-k},
\]
so the set of differences becomes
\[
R,R^2,\dots,R^m.
\]
Thus existence for some \(r<0\) is equivalent to existence for some \(r>1\). Henceforth, for \(n\ge 3\), we may assume
\[
r>1.
\]

Translate so that
\[
a_1=0,\qquad a_n=r^m.
\]

---

## 2. A useful lemma

We use the following standard exponential Diophantine lemma.

**Lemma.** Let \(x>1\). The equation
\[
x^u-x^v=1
\]
with integers \(u>v\ge 1\) has at most two solutions \((u,v)\). If it has two, then \(x\) is the unique real root of
\[
x^3-x-1=0
\]
(the plastic constant), and the two solutions are
\[
(u,v)=(3,1),\qquad (u,v)=(5,4).
\]

**Sketch of proof.**  
Write
\[
x^u-x^v=1 \iff x^v=\frac1{x^{u-v}-1}.
\]
For a fixed \(x>1\), define
\[
F(t)=\log_x\!\left(\frac1{x^t-1}\right)
\]
for real \(t>0\) with \(x^t>1\). A solution \((u,v)\) is exactly an integer \(t=u-v\) for which \(F(t)=v\) is a positive integer.

The function \(F\) is strictly decreasing and convex, and one checks that its graph can contain at most two lattice points. Solving the borderline case in which it contains two lattice points gives
\[
x^3=x+1,
\]
and the two lattice points correspond to
\[
(u,v)=(3,1),\qquad (u,v)=(5,4).
\]
This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

---

## 3. Constructions for \(n=2,3,4\)

### \(n=2\)

Take
\[
a_1=0,\qquad a_2=r
\]
for any \(r>0\). The only difference is \(r\).

---

### \(n=3\)

Let \(\varphi\) be the golden ratio,
\[
\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2},
\]
so that
\[
\varphi^2=\varphi+1,\qquad \varphi^3=\varphi^2+\varphi.
\]
Take
\[
a_1=0,\qquad a_2=\varphi,\qquad a_3=\varphi^3.
\]
Then
\[
a_2-a_1=\varphi,\qquad
a_3-a_2=\varphi^2,\qquad
a_3-a_1=\varphi^3.
\]
Thus the three differences are
\[
\varphi,\ \varphi^2,\ \varphi^3.
\]

---

### \(n=4\)

Let \(\rho\) be the plastic constant, i.e.
\[
\rho^3=\rho+1.
\]
We use the following identities:
\[
\rho^2-1=\rho^{-1},\qquad
\rho^3-1=\rho,\qquad
\rho^5-\rho^4=1.
\]
Take
\[
a_1=0,\qquad a_2=\rho^3,\qquad a_3=\rho^5,\qquad a_4=\rho^6.
\]
Then the six differences are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_2-a_1&=\rho^3,\\
a_3-a_2&=\rho^5-\rho^3=\rho^3(\rho^2-1)=\rho^2,\\
a_4-a_3&=\rho^6-\rho^5=\rho(\rho^5-\rho^4)=\rho,\\
a_3-a_1&=\rho^5,\\
a_4-a_2&=\rho^6-\rho^3=\rho^3(\rho^3-1)=\rho^4,\\
a_4-a_1&=\rho^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the six differences are
\[
\rho,\ \rho^2,\ \rho^3,\ \rho^4,\ \rho^5,\ \rho^6.
\]

Thus \(n=4\) is possible.

---

## 4. Nonexistence for \(n\ge 5\)

Assume \(n\ge 5\), and let
\[
m=\frac12 n(n-1)\ge 10.
\]
We have
\[
a_1=0,\qquad a_n=r^m.
\]

For every interior point \(a_i\) with \(2\le i\le n-1\), both
\[
a_i-a_1=a_i
\]
and
\[
a_n-a_i
\]
are pairwise differences, so both must be powers of \(r\). Thus there exist integers \(p_i,q_i\in\{1,\dots,m-1\}\) such that
\[
a_i=r^{p_i},\qquad a_n-a_i=r^{q_i}.
\]
Therefore
\[
r^{p_i}+r^{q_i}=r^m.
\]
Assume \(p_i<q_i\). Dividing by \(r^{p_i}\),
\[
1+r^{q_i-p_i}=r^{m-p_i},
\]
so
\[
r^{m-p_i}-r^{q_i-p_i}=1.
\]
Hence each interior point gives a solution \((u,v)\) of
\[
r^u-r^v=1.
\]

By the lemma, there are at most two such solutions. If there is only one, then there can be at most two possible complementary pairs, hence at most two interior points, contradicting \(n\ge 5\). Therefore there must be exactly two solutions, and by the lemma
\[
r=\rho
\]
is the plastic constant.

The two complementary pairs for the largest power \(\rho^m\) are then
\[
\{\rho^{m-5},\rho^{m-1}\}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\{\rho^{m-3},\rho^{m-2}\}.
\]
Thus every interior point must be one of the four powers
\[
\rho^{m-5},\ \rho^{m-3},\ \rho^{m-2},\ \rho^{m-1}.
\]

We now check that no choice of at least three of these four powers can give a valid \(n\ge 5\) configuration.

First note that \(\rho^4-1\) is **not** a power of \(\rho\). Indeed, from \(\rho^3=\rho+1\),
\[
\rho^4=\rho^2+\rho,
\]
so
\[
\rho^4-1=\rho^2+\rho-1.
\]
A short check gives
\[
\rho^2<\rho^4-1<\rho^3.
\]
Hence \(\rho^4-1\) is not equal to any \(\rho^k\).

Therefore the two exponents \(m-5\) and \(m-1\) cannot both appear among the interior points, because their difference would be
\[
\rho^{m-1}-\rho^{m-5}
=\rho^{m-5}(\rho^4-1),
\]
which is not a power of \(\rho\).

So the interior points can be only one of the following two 3-element sets (or a subset thereof):

### Case 1: \(\{m-5,m-3,m-2\}\)

The differences among these three points have exponents
\[
m-6,\quad m-7,\quad m-4.
\]
The complements to \(m\) contribute
\[
m-1,\quad m-2,\quad m-3.
\]
Including the endpoints \(0\) and \(m\), the full set of difference exponents is
\[
\{m-7,m-6,m-5,m-4,m-3,m-2,m-1,m\}.
\]

### Case 2: \(\{m-3,m-2,m-1\}\)

Similarly, the full set of difference exponents is again
\[
\{m-7,m-6,m-5,m-4,m-3,m-2,m-1,m\}.
\]

In both cases, since \(m\ge 10\), we have
\[
m-7\ge 3.
\]
Thus the smallest difference exponent is at least \(3\). But the required differences must include
\[
r^1=\rho^1,\qquad r^2=\rho^2,
\]
which are missing. Contradiction.

If all four exponents \(m-5,m-3,m-2,m-1\) were used, then \(m-5\) and \(m-1\) would both appear, which we already saw is impossible.

Therefore no configuration exists for \(n\ge 5\).

Let \(P(k)\) denote the property that every point of a finite set \(\mathcal F\) has at most \(k\) different scales in \(\mathcal F\).

We prove that the maximum possible size is \(2^k\).

---

### 1. Construction showing \(|\mathcal F|\ge 2^k\)

Take
\[
\mathcal F_k=\{0,1,2,\dots,2^k-1\}.
\]
For any \(x\in \mathcal F_k\) and any \(y\neq x\), the distance \(|x-y|\) is an integer between \(1\) and \(2^k-1\). Hence
\[
0\le D(x,y)\le k-1.
\]
Thus each point sees at most the \(k\) scales
\[
0,1,\dots,k-1.
\]
So a set of size \(2^k\) is possible.

---

### 2. Upper bound

We prove by induction on \(k\) that every finite set \(\mathcal F\subset\mathbb R\) satisfying \(P(k)\) has
\[
|\mathcal F|\le 2^k.
\]

For \(k=1\), if there were three points \(a<b<c\), then \(b-a\) and \(c-b\) are both at least \(2^m\) for some integer \(m\), so
\[
c-a=(b-a)+(c-b)\ge 2^{m+1}.
\]
Thus \(a\) would have at least two different scales, contradiction. Hence \(|\mathcal F|\le 2\).

Now assume the result for \(k-1\). We use the following standard splitting lemma.

#### Splitting lemma
Let \(\mathcal F\) be a finite set satisfying \(P(k)\). Then either

1. \(\mathcal F\) can be separated by a gap into two nonempty sets \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\), all elements of \(\mathcal A\) less than all elements of \(\mathcal B\), such that both \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal B\) satisfy \(P(k-1)\); or  
2. \(|\mathcal F|\le 2^k-1\).

**Sketch of proof.** Order the points as
\[
x_1<x_2<\cdots<x_n.
\]
For a cut \(i\), write
\[
L_i=\{x_1,\dots,x_i\},\qquad R_i=\{x_{i+1},\dots,x_n\}.
\]
For each point \(x_j\), consider the cuts for which the side containing \(x_j\) gives \(x_j\) at most \(k-1\) scales. If \(x_j\) has fewer than \(k\) scales in \(\mathcal F\), then every cut is good for \(x_j\). If \(x_j\) has exactly \(k\) scales, then for each scale \(s\) of \(x_j\), look at the nearest representative of that scale on the left and on the right. A scale that occurs on both sides of \(x_j\) cannot help a cut reduce the number of scales of \(x_j\); only one-sided scales matter. One checks directly that the set of good cuts for \(x_j\) is an interval of integers.

If the intersection of all these intervals is nonempty, then a cut in the intersection gives a separation into two sets each satisfying \(P(k-1)\), proving case 1.

If the intersection is empty, the interval structure forces the existence of a point \(x\) whose \(k\) scales all occur on both sides of \(x\). Let \(\mathcal L\) and \(\mathcal R\) be the points to the left and right of \(x\). For any \(y\in\mathcal L\), if \(s=D(x,y)\), choose \(z\in\mathcal R\) with \(D(x,z)=s\). Then
\[
D(y,z)=s+1,
\]
and this external scale prevents \(y\) from having \(k\) scales inside \(\mathcal L\). Thus \(\mathcal L\) satisfies \(P(k-1)\); similarly \(\mathcal R\) satisfies \(P(k-1)\). Moreover, neither side can have size \(2^{k-1}\), otherwise the equality case for \(k-1\) would force a point in \(\mathcal F\) to have \(k+1\) scales. Hence
\[
|\mathcal L|,|\mathcal R|\le 2^{k-1}-1,
\]
so
\[
|\mathcal F|\le 1+2(2^{k-1}-1)=2^k-1.
\]
This proves the lemma.

Now apply the lemma. In case 1, by the induction hypothesis,
\[
|\mathcal A|\le 2^{k-1},\qquad |\mathcal B|\le 2^{k-1},
\]
so
\[
|\mathcal F|=|\mathcal A|+|\mathcal B|\le 2^k.
\]
In case 2,
\[
|\mathcal F|\le 2^k-1<2^k.
\]
Thus in all cases,
\[
|\mathcal F|\le 2^k.
\]

If \(\mathcal F\) were infinite, choosing any \(2^k+1\) points would give a finite subset satisfying \(P(k)\), contradicting the bound above. Therefore \(\mathcal F\) is finite and bounded by \(2^k\).

Combining the construction and the upper bound, the maximum possible size is exactly \(2^k\).

So the final answer is \(\boxed{2^k}\).

a+b+c+d

\equiv \alpha+\gamma \pmod 2.
\]

If instead \(c<b\), the same argument with the roles of \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) exchanged gives the same conclusion.

Thus:

> **Every \(2\times 2\) subgrid contains either \(1\) or \(3\) odd values of \(f\).**

## 4. Bounds for \(N\)

Partition the \(100\times 100\) square
\[
0\le x,y<100
\]
into
\[
50\cdot 50=2500
\]
disjoint \(2\times 2\) blocks. Each block contains \(1\) or \(3\) odd values. Therefore
\[
2500\le N\le 7500.
\]

It remains to show that both endpoints are attainable.

## 5. Attaining \(N=2500\)

Define a total order on \(\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^2\) by lexicographic order on the key
\[
K_-(x,y)=(100x+y,\ -x).
\]
Each level \(100x+y=n\) is finite, so this is a well-order of type \(\mathbb N\). Let \(f_-\) be the corresponding rank function, with the least point having rank \(0\).

Adding \(e_1\) changes the key by
\[
(100,-1),
\]
and adding \(e_2\) changes the key by
\[
(1,0).
\]
Lexicographic order is invariant under adding a fixed vector to both keys, so \(f_-\) satisfies the required property.

Now fix \(0\le x,y<100\). The number of points \((u,v)\) with
\[
100u+v<100x+y
\]
is
\[
\sum_{u=0}^{x-1}\bigl(100(x-u)+y\bigr)+y
=50x(x+1)+(x+1)y.
\]
On the same level \(100u+v=100x+y\), the possible points are
\[
(u,\,100(x-u)+y),\qquad 0\le u\le x.
\]
Because the second key is \(-u\), smaller key means larger \(u\), so \((x,y)\) is first on its level. Hence
\[
f_-(x,y)=50x(x+1)+(x+1)y.
\]
Since \(50x(x+1)\) is even,
\[
f_-(x,y)\equiv (x+1)y\pmod 2.
\]
If \(x\) is odd, then \(x+1\) is even, so all \(100\) values in that column are even. If \(x\) is even, then \(f_-(x,y)\) is odd exactly when \(y\) is odd.

There are \(50\) even \(x\)-values and \(50\) odd \(y\)-values, so
\[
N=50\cdot 50=2500.
\]

## 6. Attaining \(N=7500\)

Now define a total order by lexicographic order on the key
\[
K_+(x,y)=(100x+y,\ x).
\]
Again this gives a well-order of type \(\mathbb N\). Let \(f_+\) be its rank function. Adding \(e_1\) changes the key by \((100,1)\), and adding \(e_2\) changes the key by \((1,0)\), so \(f_+\) satisfies the required property.

For \(0\le x,y<100\), the lower-level count is again
\[
50x(x+1)+(x+1)y.
\]
On the same level, the point \((x,y)\) now comes after the \(x\) points with smaller \(u\), so
\[
f_+(x,y)=50x(x+1)+(x+1)y+x.
\]
Thus
\[
f_+(x,y)\equiv (x+1)y+x\pmod 2.
\]
If \(x\) is even, this is odd exactly when \(y\) is odd: \(50\) odds in each even column. If \(x\) is odd, then \(x+1\) is even and the expression is always odd: \(100\) odds in each odd column.

Therefore
\[
N=50\cdot 50+50\cdot 100=2500+5000=7500.
\]

So the smallest possible value is \(2500\), and the largest possible value is \(7500\).

So the final answer is \boxed{2500,7500}.

Let \(n=2022\). We will show that the smallest possible number of initially written tuples is \(3\).

First note a useful normal form. Starting from initial tuples \(\mathbf v_1,\dots,\mathbf v_s\), every tuple that can be obtained is a coordinatewise maximum of finitely many tuples of the form

\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^s c_\ell \mathbf v_\ell,
\qquad c_\ell\in \mathbb Z_{\ge 0},
\]

with not all \(c_\ell\) zero. Indeed, addition distributes over coordinatewise maximum:

\[
\left(\bigvee_k \mathbf a_k\right)+\left(\bigvee_j \mathbf b_j\right)
=
\bigvee_{k,j}(\mathbf a_k+\mathbf b_j),
\]

and the maximum of two maxima is the maximum of the union. Conversely, any finite maximum of such sums is clearly obtainable by additions and maxima.

## 1. Two initial tuples are not enough

We first exclude \(s=1\). With one initial tuple, every coordinate value obtainable is a nonnegative integer multiple of the corresponding initial coordinate, so it cannot contain both positive and negative integers. Thus \(s\ge 2\).

Now suppose, for contradiction, that two initial tuples \(\mathbf A,\mathbf B\in\mathbb Z^n\) suffice.

For a fixed coordinate \(i\), every value that can appear in coordinate \(i\) is of the form

\[
pA_i+qB_i,\qquad p,q\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0},
\]

So we may write

\[
A_i=\varepsilon_i a_i,\qquad B_i=-\varepsilon_i b_i,
\]

\[
r_i=\frac{b_i}{a_i}>0.
\]

Fix an index \(i\), and for an integer \(M>0\) consider the tuple \(\mathbf x^{(i,M)}\) whose \(i\)-th coordinate is \(0\) and whose other coordinates are \(-M\):

\[
x^{(i,M)}_i=0,\qquad x^{(i,M)}_j=-M\quad (j\ne i).

Since its \(i\)-th coordinate is \(0\), at least one of those sums, say \(p\mathbf A+q\mathbf B\), has \(i\)-th coordinate \(0\). pA_i+qB_i=0

## 1. Excluding \(b<p\)

Assume first that \(b<p\). If \(a\ge b+1\), then since \(p\ge b+1\) and the function
\[
f(m)=(b+1)^m-m
\]
is increasing for \(m\ge1\), we have
\[
a^p\ge (b+1)^p > b!+p.
\]
Indeed,
\[
(b+1)^{b+1}>b!+b+1
\]
for \(b=1,2\) by direct check, and for \(b\ge2\),
\[
(b+1)^{b+1}>(b+1)b^b>b^b+b+1\ge b!+b+1.
\]
Thus \(a\le b\).

If \(a>1\), let \(r\) be a prime divisor of \(a\). Since \(a\le b<p\), we have \(r\le b\), so \(r\mid b!\). Reducing
\[
a^p=b!+p
\]
modulo \(r\) gives
\[
0\equiv p\pmod r,
\]
so \(r\mid p\), impossible because \(r\le b<p\). Hence \(a=1\), which is impossible. Therefore
\[
b\ge p.
\]

## 2. Consequences of \(b\ge p\)

Since \(p\mid b!\), we get
\[
a^p=b!+p\equiv 0\pmod p.
\]
By Fermat’s little theorem, \(a^p\equiv a\pmod p\), so \(p\mid a\). Write
\[
a=pc
\]
with \(c\in\mathbb Z_{>0}\). Then
\[
p^p c^p=b!+p,
\]
so
\[
b!=p\bigl(p^{p-1}c^p-1\bigr).
\]
The factor in parentheses is congruent to \(-1\pmod p\), so
\[
v_p(b!)=1.
\]
Hence
\[
p\le b<2p.
\]

Now let
\[
M=\frac{b!}{p}.
\]
Since \(c^p=\dfrac{b!+p}{p^p}=\dfrac{M+1}{p^{p-1}}\), it remains to bound \(M\). Write \(b=p+n\) with \(0\le n\le p-1\). Then
\[
M=\frac{b!}{p}=(p-1)!\prod_{k=1}^n(p+k).
\]
Since \((p-1)!<p^{p-1}\) and each factor \(p+k\le b\), with at most \(p-1\) factors, we get
\[
M<p^{p-1}b^{p-1}.
\]
Thus
\[
c^p=\frac{M+1}{p^{p-1}}\le b^{p-1}<b^p,
\]
so
\[
c<b.
\]

If a prime \(r\ne p\) divided \(c\), then \(r\le c<b\), so \(r\mid b!\). But reducing
\[
b!=p(p^{p-1}c^p-1)
\]
modulo \(r\) gives
\[
0\equiv -p\pmod r,
\]
impossible. Therefore \(c\) has no prime divisors other than possibly \(p\), so
\[
c=p^t.

Since \(c<b<2p\), we must have \(t\le1\). Hence
\[
c=1\quad\text{or}\quad c=p.

\[
b!=p^p-p=p(p^{p-1}-1).

\[

so \(b=4\). This gives
\[
(a,b,p)=(3,4,3).

\[
v_2(b!)=v_2(p^{p-1}-1).

\[

We view the board as the grid graph \(G\), whose vertices are the \(n^2\) cells and whose edges join side-adjacent cells.  
Given a filling with \(1,2,\dots,n^2\), direct every edge from the smaller number to the larger number. Then a good path is exactly a directed path whose first vertex has in-degree \(0\), i.e. a local minimum.

Let \(m\) be the number of edges of the \(n\times n\) grid:
\[
m=2n(n-1)=2n^2-2n.
\]

## 1. Lower bound

In any finite directed acyclic graph, every vertex is reachable from some source (in-degree \(0\)).

Take any directed edge
\[
u\to v.
\]
Choose a directed path from a source to \(u\), and append the edge \(u\to v\). This gives a good path whose last edge is \(u\to v\).

If two different edges produce the same good path, then the last edge of that path would be two different edges, impossible. Hence every directed edge gives a distinct good path of length at least \(2\).

Finally, there is at least one source, and its one-vertex path is a good path not counted above. Therefore the number \(P\) of good paths satisfies
\[
P\ge m+1=2n^2-2n+1.
\]

## 2. Construction attaining the bound

It remains to show that \(m+1\) is attainable.

We construct a labeling with the following structure:

- there is exactly one local minimum, say \(r\);
- some cells are local maxima (sinks);
- if the sink cells are removed, the remaining cells form a tree;
- all edges inside this tree are directed away from \(r\), and every edge between the tree and a sink is directed into the sink.

Such a configuration is easy to obtain inductively by adding one row and one column at a time: the new \(L\)-shaped border is a path, and we mark a suitable set of its cells as new sinks so that every remaining piece of the border attaches to the old tree in exactly one cell. This keeps the non-sink cells a tree and keeps the sinks independent.

Now count the good paths in such a configuration.

Let \(T\) be the tree of non-sink cells. Since the edges of \(T\) are directed away from the unique source \(r\), every vertex of \(T\) has exactly one directed path from \(r\) to it. Thus these give \(|T|\) good paths.

Every edge entering a sink has exactly one good path ending with it: take the unique path from \(r\) to its tail in \(T\), then take the edge into the sink. There are
\[
m-(|T|-1)
\]
such edges, because the tree \(T\) uses \(|T|-1\) edges.

Hence the total number of good paths is
\[
|T|+\bigl(m-(|T|-1)\bigr)=m+1.
\]

Thus the lower bound is sharp.

Since
\[
m+1=2n(n-1)+1=2n^2-2n+1,
\]
the smallest possible number of good paths is

\[
\boxed{2n^2-2n+1}.
\]

So the final answer is \(\boxed{2n^2-2n+1}\).

\[
999=2m+1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad m=499.
\]

We will show that the maximum possible number of visited squares is

\[
(2m)^2=998^2=996004.
\]

---

## 1. Upper bound

In a cyclic route, every visited square has exactly two neighbours in the route. Since consecutive moves must be perpendicular, at each visited square one of the two route-neighbours is horizontal and the other is vertical.

Therefore, in each row, the visited squares are paired by horizontal route-edges. Each such horizontal edge joins two consecutive columns, one odd-numbered and one even-numbered. Hence in every row,

\[
\#\{\text{visited squares in odd columns}\}
=
\#\{\text{visited squares in even columns}\}.
\]

The board has \(500\) odd columns and \(499\) even columns. Let \(U\) be the set of unvisited squares. In any fixed row, if \(u_o\) and \(u_e\) denote the numbers of unvisited squares in odd and even columns, then

\[
500-u_o=499-u_e
\]

so

\[
u_o-u_e=1.
\]

Similarly, in every column,

\[
\#\{\text{unvisited squares in odd rows}\}
-
\#\{\text{unvisited squares in even rows}\}
=1.
\]

Now count unvisited squares according to the parity of row and column:

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
 & \text{odd column} & \text{even column}\\ \hline
\text{odd row} & A & B\\
\text{even row} & C & D
\end{array}
\]

Summing the row conditions over odd rows and even rows gives

\[
A-B=500,\qquad C-D=499.
\]

Summing the column conditions over odd columns and even columns gives

\[
A-C=500,\qquad B-D=499.
\]

Thus

\[
B=D+499,\qquad C=D+499,\qquad A=D+999.
\]

So the total number of unvisited squares is

\[
A+B+C+D
=
(D+999)+(D+499)+(D+499)+D
=
4D+1997.
\]

Since \(D\ge 0\), at least \(1997\) squares must be unvisited. Therefore the number of visited squares is at most

\[
999^2-1997
=
998001-1997
=
996004.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
996004=998^2.
\]

---

## 2. Sharpness of the bound

The bound is attainable by a standard zigzag spiral construction.

For a \((2m+1)\times(2m+1)\) board, one can build concentric “limp-rook” rings. The \(k\)-th ring is a cyclic non-intersecting limp route of length

\[
